newsitem.title: GERMANY: Leading German Eurosceptic a Bavarian populist.
newsitem.headline: Leading German Eurosceptic a Bavarian populist.

text.p: Edmund Stoiber, the Bavarian state premier whose boisterous Euroscepticism has taken centre stage in Germany's debate over Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU), is a dogged populist who calls himself "a 150 percenter".
His many critics can be less flattering, preferring to call the hard-hitting conservative "the blond hatchet", "Edmund Thatcher" or "the Bavarian pit bull terrier".

Chancellor Helmut Kohl has avoided uttering in public any of the many names for the man who threatens to upset his dream of a single currency in 1999 with his ever-louder calls for the strictest interpretation of the Maastricht criteria.
But Kohl's latest comment on Stoiber, widely reported in the press, gave a taste of how strained their relations are: "He's going to get a smack on the head."

Stoiber, 55, has emerged as the self-styled defender of the deutsche mark, the Cassandra who insists the new single currency must fulfil the strict Maastricht criteria exactly or Germany's conservatives will face a terrible backlash from angry voters.

His single-minded campaign for Teutonic precision in assessing each country's euro qualifications has forced Finance Minister Theo Waigel to uphold Maastricht's 3.0 deficit target rigidly long after almost everyone else has given up on it.

From his bully pulpit as premier of the prosperous and sometimes eccentric southern state, Stoiber has campaigned for an EMU delay and threatened to break ranks to vote against Kohl's pet project when it comes up for approval next year.

None of this fits Kohl's gameplan, which sees EMU starting on time in 1999 whether EU partners Germany and France meet the target of a three percent deficit-to-GDP ratio or -- as looks much more likely -- end up a few 10ths of a percent above it.
But Stoiber, who climbed up the slippery ladder of state politics with the help of the late and legendary Bavarian leader Franz Josef Strauss, has other scenarios in mind.

The premier's gaze is fixed on Bavaria's state election in early September 1998, where splinter parties like the anti-foreigner Republicans or the grass-roots "Free Voter Associations" could spoil his absolute majority and possibly even throw out his Christian Social Union (CSU) after decades of unchallenged power.
His hard line also helps in his rivalry with Waigel, who Stoiber hopes will be so linked with the unpopular euro that he can replace the finance minister as CSU party chairman.

"Stoiber's anti-euro line is not just a cheap way to make a name at the expense of Helmut Kohl or Theo Waigel, neither of whom could be called his friend," the Frankfurter Rundschau daily commented on Monday.
"His political destiny depends on it, so he won't simply knuckle under just because Helmut Kohl wrinkles his brow in annoyance."
Die Welt added: "The fact he smashes some European policy china in the process doesn't bother Stoiber much."

It bothers Kohl but he can't do much about it. Stoiber's CSU is the Bavarian sister party to Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and its success is crucial to the chancellor's re-election drive in the general election which comes just a few weeks after the Bavarian state election.
"Kohl can't answer him in public as he would like to," one CDU strategist explained. "We need him to win next year."

Stoiber, who came in as a "Mr Clean" premier in 1993 to halt a frightening slide in the CSU's once-unassailable power, is a calculating tactician who regularly resorts to beerhall populism to please his deeply conservative voters.
Standing up to Bonn is part of the game, whether it be in demanding crucifixes in public schools, tightening a national abortion law or demanding an EMU delay.
According to local rules, punching away at Bonn while wrapped in Bavaria's blue-and-white chequered flag is often more important than actually winning the fight.
"Stoiber has to go for broke," Berlin's Tageszeitung commented. "The euro is a godsend. There is no other issue that can create so much havoc at such a low price."
A lawyer by training, Stoiber was CSU general secretary, Strauss's chief of staff and state interior minister before becoming the uncrowned king of Bavarian politics.

He frequently appears in public with his wife and two attractive student-age daughters in a pointed contrast to Waigel, whose divorce and remarriage to former ski star Irene Epple still angers many pious Catholics in Bavaria.
